#3665. Grand Theft Auto 6: The Kotaku Review

GTA 6 is a game that at times feels almost embarrassingly expensive and extravagant. I cleaned a boat with a pressure washer and watched the suds build up realistically in the concrete below my characterâs flip-flops. I ran through a tram station and spotted over 100 different NPCs milling about, all unique and all moving. Hair gets wet. Sweat builds up on backs. Even for Rockstar, the master of tiny details, GTA 6 is overflowing with examples of what happens when you let a studio work on one game for a decade. Itâs a lot, but it all serves the purpose of creating a virtual world that players can truly get lost in.Â

Iâve put over 150 hours into GTA 6 on PlayStation 5 Pro, and I expect Iâll spend even more time in this digital recreation of Florida and Miami, as thereâs so much to do and see in Vice City. I doubt most players will see half of it. I bet I wonât ever see it all.Â

GTA 6 is a massive third-person open-world game, like Rockstarâs previous offerings. It merges the slower pace and slice-of-life mechanics from Red Dead Redemption 2 with the urban sprawl and crime-movie feel of GTA IV and GTA V. Itâs a more grounded journey than its predecessors, one which requires more planning and consideration if you want to survive and succeed as modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, robbing small stores as you work your way up to bigger scores, like banks. Itâs often a tougher game than any past GTA, but in a way that rewards skill and patience. Or bravery, stupidity, and luck.Â

I have quibbles about some clunky controls and some story pacing problems in the gameâs later chapters, but like crappy cupholders in a million-dollar supercar, they donât really get in the way of what’s here. Instead, they’re minor issues to point at as I hit the gas and go 200 MPH with the radio blasting.Â

The best part of Grand Theft Auto 6 isnât what I expected. It’s not the crime, or the action, or the massive world to explore, though all of those parts are excellent and better than ever. The real standout of GTA 6, the part of the game that kept me hooked and which I wonât forget anytime soon, is its central duo, Jason and Lucia.

Not only do they have very different motivations than past GTA protagonists, wanting to create a better life for themselves and escape their life of crime instead of vying to become crime lords or get revenge, but they are easily Rockstarâs most fully fleshed-out, believable, and relatable characters.

At the start of the game, Jason and Lucia are separated after a short relationship. Lucia tried to rob a payday loan place after breaking up with Jason and, in the process, got arrested. This moment has huge ramifications for both of their lives and ultimately pulls them together early on in GTA 6âs runtime.

Jason, an Army vet, is more reserved than your average GTA protagonist. Heâs a loyal man who’s conflicted about the things he does to get by and try to make things better for himself and Lucia. A lot of people tell Jason heâs a good guy, but heâs never sure if he really is. Meanwhile, Lucia, a petty thief living paycheck to paycheck, knows sheâs flawed and doesnât care nearly as much as Jason about that fact. Sheâs more focused on improving her life by any means and has a bigger goal that drives her to take bigger risks.Â

Together they balance each other out, with Jason often acting as a voice of reason and Lucia pushing him to strive for more. Their dynamic is unlike anything Iâve seen in a Rockstar-developed game, and thanks to some stellar writing and performances, I found myself deeply caring about these two criminals just trying to make it.Â

Throughout the entire run of GTA 6, Jason and Lucia interact as you would expect two real people who care for each other would. They joke with each other, comment on events happening around them, share secrets, and help each other when they can.Â

Spending time with them is never annoying. Neither Lucia nor Jason pesters the player when youâre hanging around with them in the open world. Sometimes they might point out that you missed a turn or a possible way to sneak into a gang-infested hideout. This never felt like some annoying video-gamey handholding, just a couple working together.Â

While Jason and Lucia are both skilled at stealing cars, shooting guns, and running around causing chaos, they arenât always treated as equals in the world. While playing as Lucia, I was hit on by random assholes and catcalled by men on the street. It wasnât constant, but it happened enough that it was impossible to ignore. Some characters will also doubt Luciaâs abilities, but never question Jasonâs skills as a murderous criminal. It adds an intriguing wrinkle to playing as either character. Lucia feels like she has to work harder to prove herself among her criminal peers. Jason often has her back in these scenarios, but lets her hold her own, and she does so with sharp words and strong punches.Â

Even outside of when they directly speak to each other to tell stories or give feedback, the other’s presence is always felt, sometimes in small gestures, like one holding the door for the other as they enter a building. And sometimes, depending on how you handle their relationship, through more intimate moments that either Jason or Lucia, regardless of whether the player is controlling them, can initiate when theyâre feeling ready to fool around.Â

One time while I was playing as Jason, after spending all day and most of the night with Lucia, we came home, and I couldnât even get through the door before both of them were on top of each other. If you were wondering: Jason and Lucia fuck a lot in this game, assuming you play them as a couple, which I did.Â

It didnât take long for me to fall in love with Jason and Lucia. And I spent the entire game rooting for them, even as their situation became more dangerous and desperate, largely due to factors outside of their control.Â

While Jason and Luciaâs relationship, be it platonic or romantic depending on your choices, never loses steam or feels like it stops evolving, GTA 6âs main overarching narrative of criminal conspiracy and mayhem does start to falter in the back half.

In a later chapter of the story, the momentum that had carried everything forward up until that point fades. It feels like GTA 6âs story begins spinning its wheels at this point. By the end, the narrative picks back up, and the stakes grow even larger as Jason and Lucia rely on themselves to take on the world. But even when the story started to lose steam, and I felt myself wondering how many more missions Iâd have to do before something big happened, Jason and Lucia were there to keep me going. Lucia doing an impersonation of Jasonâs deep voice always made me chuckle, as did any time Jason gave her crap about her bad driving after I crashed another car.Â

Just know there are multiple endings, and after seeing two of them in my time with the game, I can confirm that how you play and what choices you make can have a huge impact on how things turn out. Happy endings areâ¦not common in this line of work, but not impossible.Â

Even if the rest of GTA 6 didnât work, Jason, Lucia, and their relationship would still carry it across the finish line. Thankfully, the rest of Grand Theft Auto 6 is very good, too.Â

The second-best part of GTA 6, behind our Bonnie and Clyde duo, is the world of Leonida, the state that Vice City is located in. It is the most detailed, gorgeous, and alive open world Iâve ever experienced in a video game.Â

GTA 6 starts off in the southern part of the map, far away from the skyscrapers and glitz of Vice City. You can almost see it in the distance from the small coastal town where GTA 6 begins. Itâs the kind of scale Iâve not really felt before in an open-world game. And all that spaceâ¦it ainât empty.Â

It feels like every inch of GTA 6 is filled with life. With movement. Withâ¦something. Even areas like the huge swamp, which at first glance might seem empty, reveal themselves to be filled with detail and specificity. That swamp, for instance, is teeming with creatures, big and small. The wind rustles the leaves of every tree and plant around. Planes fly overhead at different altitudes. I ran deeper in and stumbled upon a giant snake with a dead body in its mouth. Later, I found a crashed plane smuggling drugs. In the distance, I spotted dark clouds forming and bursts of lightning. Rain was coming. And later, I watched a lightning bolt crash into the woods and start a small fire.Â

All this happened in the span of an hour in one relatively small section of the swamp, itself a small portion of the larger world. Itâs at times overwhelming. Driving through the city, which I didnât reach until nearly a dozen hours into the game, I felt guilty about all the life and detail I was speeding by at 100 MPH.Â

I was also much more focused on the road than in past GTA games. The streets in GTA 6 arenât as wide as those in GTA V, and there are far more cars on the road. Crashing into these other drivers can quickly damage your vehicle, making it harder to steer or accelerate. But I didnât find any of this annoying. Instead, it made it satisfying to weave through traffic to escape police. The act of just driving a car is so much more exciting than it’s ever been in the franchise. It felt like a real skill Iâd developed after a few hours and one which I always enjoyed using, making long road trips across the map feel less like a chore and more like an opportunity to explore more of the game.Â

All of these changes to driving and the roads in GTA 6 also forced me to sometimes slow down or stop, giving me more time to take in all the atmosphere and detail packed into the game.Â And I do recommend slowing down whenever possible and just soaking in Vice City and Leonida. GTA 6 is a game that truly rewards exploration and poking around. Even 150 hours in, Iâm still encountering new random events, side characters, and more.

One day in Vice City, as I was walking down the street, I entered a small convenience store to buy some food and boost my health stat. But inside, I found a criminal behind the cash register and a dead body on the floor near them. I held the left trigger to lock onto the robber, a young woman, and questioned her about what was happening. She said to mind my own business and leave. I taunted her next. This was a mistake. The young woman robbing the small store was armed with a gun and pointed it at me. I quickly drew my own pistol, and we started shooting. A second later, she was dead. I grabbed the cashâI mean, I couldnât just leave it there on the groundâand ran out the back where I found the robberâs car. In the trunk were drugs and ammo. Before I could look around more, I heard sirens. The cops were coming. I quickly hopped a fence and ran by some people who werenât happy that I was running through their backyard.Â

Just another day in Leonida. Iâve truly never experienced an open world like this before, and every time I think Iâve seen it all or canât be more impressed by it than I already am, Iâm quickly proven wrong.Â

One night, I climbed the gameâs tallest mountain, and when I reached the top, it was nighttime. Vice City and its sprawl were laid out in front of me, thousands of twinkling lights and bright dots floating in the darkness miles and miles away. Lucia took it in and exclaimed to Jason that it was gorgeous. He agreed. So did I.Â

But it ainât just a big pretty world with lots of moving parts. Itâs also Rockstarâs attempt to simulate as much of life in Leonida as possible. Youâll find over 600 stores to shop at, gyms to work out in, gun ranges to visit, golf courses to play on, zoos to explore, gas stations to rob, bars to chill in, animals to hunt, mod shops to improve cars at, and even working buses and trains with actual schedules and passengers.Â

You can, and I did, just live out a normal day in the life of Jason and Lucia, freely swapping between them to see what the other was up to at any time.Â

During one session as Jason, I hit the gym early in the morning, then hopped in my off-road car and headed north to do some hunting. When I wanted to shake things up, I swapped over to Lucia, and a few seconds later I was playing as her. She was chilling on a beach, and a friend of hersâthey each have their own social livesâtexted, checking in on me. I replied and then got hit on by a random asshole. So I taunted him until he called me a bitch and left. A moment later I swapped back to Jason, and he was at a nearby gas station with his gun out. I took the hint and hunted a different kind of animal, and came away $450 richer. Other times Iâd switch to find them watching TV, chatting up a random NPC, or driving around the city.Â

The incredibly realistic graphics and the focus on simulating not just the fact that your partnerâs life continues when you arenât near them, but that they exist in an entire living world, one where you can gain weight, get tired, and ride the bus, do at times clash with the parts of the game where Rockstar clearly didnât want to annoy people with the sorts of inconveniences that can emerge out of realism.Â

For example, every store in the game is open 24 hours a day. This means you can walk into a barber shop at 3 am and get a haircut. To the gameâs credit, the shop was empty besides the employees at that time, something I found true in other stores and locations at odd hours. But these bits of video gameâness stood out all the more because the world was otherwise so lifelike.

All this simulation, fancy visuals, and scale does have a cost. The game runs at 30FPS, even on PS5 Pro. And in some areas of the map, like on the packed streets of Vice City, I noticed framerate drops. I also spotted slowdown during large firefights with police. It never became unplayable, but it does make me curious to see how this game will look on a powerful PC.Â

If youâve reached this point and are starting to wonder if this is still a GTA game, donât worry; thereâs plenty of shooting, robbing, car theft, murder, and action to be had. But this time around, crime isnât as easy as it has been in the past, which makes it so much more rewarding and fun.Â

Police in GTA 6 are not to be underestimated. They can quickly overwhelm Lucia and Jason and will share important details about the couple with each other on the radio, making it harder to evade officers looking for you. It pays to keep a change of clothing in your trunk and store large weapons in there too, unless you want every cop in the area to come calling after people spot an armed person matching a suspected robberâs description.Â

Even hitting a small gas station is thrilling because of how much smarter police are and how much more challenging GTA 6 can be.

You can walk into a store, pull out a gun, kill the clerk, take his money, and run. But the surveillance camera will record you, people in the area will report your location, and cops will be after you quicker due to the murder and gunfire.Â

Instead, you should sneak in through the back, put on a mask, destroy any camera recordings, disable the alarm, crack open the safe, and then head out front to force the clerk to hand over the cash. Then bail, leaving him alive, and enter your car, which you smartly parked further away from the scene. Once you reach a safe spot, you can change your clothes if you have any heat, and then drive by the cops rushing to the scene without any of them suspecting a thing.Â

Pulling off perfect crimes like that, even on a small scale, is so rewarding.Â

Even the simple act of stealing a car in GTA 6 is more engaging and fun than it’s ever been in past games. Some cars are easy to just pop the lock on, hop in, and hotwire. But other cars demand you use a slim jim to shimmy open the lock via a simple, quick mini-game. And still other, fancier cars require Jason and Lucia to use a key cloner to gain access, which is also pulled off via a mini-game. Those cars canât even be hotwired, meaning for a large chunk of the game you have to avoid the coolest cars in Vice City and settle for rust buckets and unlocked sedans. And even some of those cars have trackers that make it easier for police to find you later, and harder to modify and sell them to shops around the city.Â

But like the slimmer roadways and more punishing crashes, this change to the GTA formula didnât frustrate me. On the contrary, I found it so much more exciting to steal cars in GTA 6. I became skilled at spotting cars that would likely be easier to steal than others without needing to use the car-scanning app included on your in-game phone. (Thereâs also an Instagram-like social media app on there, and you can text and call other characters, including your partner.)Â

And if you just canât help yourself, well, you can always steal any car driving around the map by yanking its driver out if you really want that badass Banshee. Jason and Lucia can also drive boats, planes, helicopters, dirt bikes, semi-trucks, airboats, buses, bulldozers, jet skis, andâif youâre brave enough to enter the gameâs military baseâeven a jet or tank. Good luck with that.Â

"Welcome to Vice City. Enjoy spending your next few years exploring every inch of this place!"

Third-person open-world action game with two playable characters and some RPG-like systems, cover-based shooting, and lots of customization options.

Jason and Lucia, the open world, challenging police, skillful driving, mission variety, multiple endings, and the music.

Some clunky controls, performance issues in big fights, and a back half that loses some narrative oomph.

152 hours. Finished main story campaign, saw two different endings, tried out most side activities, completed most side missions, and explored nearly the entire map.

Gunplay, like other parts of the GTA formula, is also more challenging, but better, than ever in GTA 6. Thatâs largely because Rockstar has moved away from the easy auto-aim nonsense of GTA V. Now, combat plays out more like it did in Max Payne 3, with a focus on manual aiming and landing headshots or, if you want to avoid killing people and being labeled a psycho by the in-game criminal profile system, shooting people in the kneecaps. (That profile system can change how characters react and how aggressive police will be when chasing you down.)Â

Guns also feel louder and more powerful. When a robbery goes wrong and bullets start flying, it’s scary and tense, and I always wanted to get out of there as soon as possible. You canât take too much damage before it becomes a problem, so shootouts are risky, but not impossible, to survive. Sometimes, Iâd just wing a cop or gang member in the arm, and theyâd realistically fall back, giving me enough time to slip away before they got back up and started shooting again.Â

Alongside all these moving parts and systems, a classic Rockstar problem is back in GTA 6: clunky controls.Â

Sometimes Iâd want to loot a body, but instead Jason would try to enter a nearby car. Other times Iâd want to reload my weapon, but Iâd kick someone instead. Getting objects out of trunks can be a real pain in the ass as context-sensitive button prompts appear and disappear based on where your character is looking.

I also occasionally found the controls a bit hard to keep straight. Every button on the gamepad does something; oftentimes, multiple actions are mapped to one button or a submenu. I still sometimes forget which d-pad button to hold to swap between Lucia and Jason during the heat of combat.Â

Still, anytime I had issues with the story or some clunky controls, Iâd turn a corner and discover a whole new section of this incredibly detailed world, quickly forgetting about those minor issues. As I said, crappy cup holders donât make a Bugatti any less fun to drive or impressive to sit in. And like those hyper-expensive and perfectly tuned supercars, GTA 6 feels like it was crafted by masters who’ve been making these kinds of open-world games for a long time and are better at it than any other studio by a very wide margin.Â

Adding to the feeling that Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterclass in open-world game design are the missions. Yes, there are still the classic GTA missions that have you driving somewhere, shooting or stealing stuff, and then driving back to wrap it up. But so many missions in GTA 6 are very different from that usual formula.

A very early mission doesnât even involve guns or crime. Instead, Jason and his buddy Cal just clean up the living room, move a TV, get high, drink beer, and play video games together. We learn a lot about these two and how they care for each other in that moment, and nary a gun was fired or a murder committed.Â

But there are still plenty of big action-packed missions, and these, too, offer up experiences that arenât the usual GTA fare. A later mission involving a heist that spins out of control had my heart racing as the tension ramped up, and when all hell broke loose, GTA 6âs incredible world and improved combat were on full display.Â

Another mission involved a massive shootout that started on the street and worked its way through a building and onto a highway. During that whole fight, I was able to find my own way up, and when the game asked me to escape, I was free to do so in any car I wanted.Â

Thereâs a lot more flexibility in GTA 6âs missions, too. At one point, I was told to chase down a drug runner in a boat. The game asked me to hop on a dirt bike and follow it via a service road. Instead, I hopped into a small speedboat and the game justâ¦ rolled on, even commenting on my change of plans and changing up the objective on the fly. The person I was chasing even seemed to have different voice lines based on my choice.Â

GTA 6 is constantly reacting to your choices and actions, both in missions and when just out in the open world. It makes everything you do feel more meaningful and important, and it makes GTA 6 feel less restrictive than GTA IV and GTA V.Â

I also appreciated how experimental and creative GTA 6 can be in some of its missions. During one mission, Jason gets drugged and has to fight off tons of armed thugs. But as you run around and shoot, the world and the lights in it pulse with the music. Another mission involves Jason and Lucia robbing a bunch of tiny stores, and this is presented as a playable montage that hops from moment to moment seamlessly as a classic rock song that Rockstarâs embargo forbids me from naming plays in the background.Â

The licensed soundtrack is incredible, with a massive list of music across the gameâs various radio stations. And this time around, you can also listen to multiple in-game podcasts, either in your car or on foot via headphones. One is a true-crime podcast hosted by two terrible people that includes an episode dedicated to the serial killer side character in GTA IV.Â

Just like in past GTA games, thereâs a ton of content to watch on the TV, too, including multiple episodes of animated TV shows parodying American culture, politics, and police. Thereâs also a game show about people identifying men by looking at just their penises. Some of these shows advertise in the world or on social media, too. And characters will talk about shows and other parts of the world and post about them as the game goes on. Itâs just one more thing that makes the world of Vice City feel less like a static playground and more like a real place that reacts to my actions and crimes.

During one random event, I encountered a polar bear being transported to a zoo. I helped some protestors stop the truck, and the bear escaped, killing a few people and then running off in the city. Later, I saw a news article and a social media post about the bear. Another time I saw a viral clip of a stuntman doing a backflip at a football game and ripping open his suit to reveal his penis. Later on, I met that guy selling a cryptocoin and helped him out before he screwed me and some investors over, leading to news stories and social media posts from the tech company and its angry customers. And then a radio broadcast summed all this up via a short news piece while I was driving around later. This kind of stuff happens all the time in GTA 6, and it makes the whole world feel so alive and reactive.Â

This is the kind of stuff that elevates Rockstarâs open world above so many others. Sure, others might look good and feature fun missions. But Rockstarâs games are still the best at playing with the player and reacting to them. And GTA 6 takes this to a whole different level.

I also must shout out GTA 6âs original score, composed by Justice. Their soundtrack is a wild and wonderful mix of electronic dance, â80s funk, and rock guitars that permeates the game and adds so much to it. Strange moments are made weirder by their music. Silly moments are made even sillier and heartbreaking moments more painful.Â Iâll be jamming out to the gameâs score for weeks, I suspect. Even if you donât end up liking GTA 6 or even playing it, Justiceâs soundtrack is worth checking out.Â

A complete review of Grand Theft Auto 6 feels both impossible and in some ways unnecessary. For folks who see reviews as simply text that tells them if a game is worth buying or not, well, this is a game that doesnât need any help convincing people to buy it. And a game of this scale is hard to distill and evaluate, even with thousands of words. I sit here and feel like Iâve left out so much of what GTA 6 is.Â

Grand Theft Auto 6 is not the kind of game we get very often. Itâs a massive experience that is filled with more content and more ideas than some entire game franchises.Â

I had high expectations for Grand Theft Auto 6. This much time and money being poured into one video game leads to a lot of hype. Yet GTA 6 surprised me by not just meeting those expectations, but often exceeding them.Â

Jason and Lucia feel like a real couple and I loved rooting for them as they tried to escape the shitty hand they’d been dealt. The world is not just massive but also reactive, and feels the closest a video game has ever gotten to truly recreating all the vibes, life, and details youâd expect from a real place. The action is better than ever, but GTA 6âs quiet moments are really where the game leapfrogs over anything seen in a past GTA entry. And it all comes together to deliver something that truly makes the long wait feel both worth it and absolutely necessary.Â

There were nights when Iâd stay up far too late playing this game, not because I was crunching to finish it before the review embargo, but because I just didnât want to put the controller down.Â

GTA 6 is a truly remarkable game. A masterpiece of open-world design that brings forward the best parts of all of Rockstarâs past games into one billion-dollar adventure that is unlike anything Iâve played before. Itâs a game Iâll be playing for years, and I canât wait to talk about it with others.Â

#3664. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3663. World of Warcraft: Forever's in-game economy has been ravaged by an exploit that allowed players to farm thousands of gold

World of Warcraft: Forever has suffered its first economic nightmare, as a dungeon farm exploit has left some players with thousands of gold in their bags while the vast majority of players are barely above their first hundred.

This exploit was quickly and quietly hotfixed by Blizzard, but not before a currently-unknown number of players were able to make out like bandits. In basic terms, the new Blackmaw Hold dungeon includes several packs of non-elite, easy to kill enemies right at the start of the dungeon. Prior to the hotfix, the loot drop tables for these enemies were incorrect, and worth vastly more in terms of gold than they should have. Keen-eyed players spotted this but kept it quiet, running into the dungeon and quickly killing off these early mobs and resetting the dungeon every hour.

This was possible on every class, and according to Twitch streamer Ziqo, allowed players to farm out hundreds of gold in a few hours. He is seen streaming with over 4,000 gold - and claims other streamers made out with more than that.

For an idea of how much money that is, one of the most expensive things a player will likely buy on their character throughout the original Classic World of Warcraft is the expert riding skill. It takes a long time to save up for, and stands as a major accomplishment in the life of a character. It costs around 900 gold. These players, in just a few days of dedicated grinding, will have been able to pay this price several times over.

Looking at community hubs for the game (Reddit or the official World of Warcraft forums), regular players are demanding Blizzard take action - going further than just the already-deployed hotfix. Maya on the WoW forum wants the ill-gotten gold to be removed and for players to be banned who made use of the Blackmaw Hold exploit, writing: "Remove the gold or I and many others will just quit. This is worse than the bots at this point."

Flnrodi on Reddit, referring to streamers who took advantage of this exploit, wrote: "Not sure what to say. The fact that he did this all offstream says enough that [Ziqo] (and others) knew that this is not intended and 100 percent considered an exploit. Personally, I think there should be some kind of punishment and definitely all the gold [should be] revoked."

You may be wondering why this is such a big deal? So what if a few players can get fancy mounts faster, or snatch up some really good gear on the player auction house? Well, exorbitant sums of money in the hands of a few players can have a massive impact on a server's economy. You could, for example, use your newfound wealth to flip every listing of a certain rare resource on the auction house and mark the price up significantly for profit, which obviously inflates the price for regular players. Likewise, you can out-bid other players for rare and powerful BOE items, which in turn raises the prices of those as sellers may find they can make more cash than they could off such drops prior to the exploit.

This all has an inflationary effect, and could push a server's economy to a more expensive level faster than it otherwise would. Even if this effect isn't so drastic, these players can essentially gear out multiple characters in fantastic gear without putting in the hours, or out-bid the rest of the community on the Black Market Auction House for rare and largely unparalleled special loot.

The counter argument against punitive measures is that these players didn't cheat. They didn't buy gold from real-money-traders, nor did they plug in some external tool to give them an unfair advantage over others. They simply put in the time to get to around level 55, ran a dungeon, and killed mobs repeatedly for valuable drops. Would it have been a good thing to flag the exploit the moment they found out about it? Sure. But once other players at your level take advantage of it, and no strict ruling around whether doing so is punishable, it's arguably in a player's best interest to join in while the going is good.

As of writing, there's been no official word from Blizzard on what it intends to do beyond fixing the exploit. Given the required level to take on Blackmaw Hold, the number of exploiters cannot be too large, and the sheer amount of gold they gained in a small amount of time should make them easy to flag. Rolling back their accounts and reverting the gold they gained back to a pre-exploit amount certainly appears to be a popular option. Whether Blizzard actually does so, or enforces other punishments, is the big question.

Blizzard suspends World of Warcraft: Forever gold exploit abusers, puts trading blocks on their accounts and removes ill-gotten funds for good measure

As a Disneyland expert and superfan, there are a few items on my bucket list that I know I’ll probably never do. Those include dining at Club 33 and getting a chance to sleep inside Sleeping Beauty’s Castle. It turns out, there’s another thing that’s so exclusive I didn’t even know it was an option: sleep in Walt’s former Disneyland apartment over the newly updated Pirates of the Caribbean attraction.

While appearing on the orange carpet at the slime-obsessed 2026 Kids’ Choice Awards, Once Upon a Time princess and beloved Zootopia actress Ginnifer Goodwin revealed that she is one of the lucky few who have been able to cross that item off her hypothetical bucket list. And from the sound of it, it was an amazing experience! During her interview with Hollywood ReelTime, Goodwin said:

I’ve gone around the park, after midnight in like a robe and slippers.

First, Goodwin gets to play the original Disney Princess Snow White in the hit ABC drama Once Upon A Time, and then she gets to voice Zootopia's Judy Hopps, one of the most beloved animated rabbits. And now, she gets to go to Disneyland whenever she wants and get to stay the night in the park. It's not like I’m totally not jealous or anything! Seriously, though, what I love is that she can appreciate the privilege, given she's a fellow Disney fanatic. Check out this recap from her late 2025 trip to Walt Disney World Resort:

A post shared by Ginnifer Goodwin (@ginnifergoodwin)

Most Disneyland fans are likely aware of Walt’s apartment above the firehouse on Main Street, which guests previously were able to visit through a paid guided tour. However, many might not know that the space above the Pirates of the Caribbean attraction was also an apartment built for Walt and his family to stay and entertain guests at, since the aforementioned firehouse apartment was too small. Unfortunately, Disney passed before the suite was completed, and his brother opted to halt construction.

It wasn’t until 2006, when Disneyland ran the “Year of a Million Dreams” promotion, that his dreams came to fruition. Thanks to the plans Walt Disney left behind, the space was turned into a suite that was made available to a randomly selected guest of the park. When the promotion ended, it became a space only Disney elite, like Goodwin and her family, could access.

I’m All In On Zootopia Director’s Response To The Fans Who Want Romance Between Judy And Nick

Unfortunately, for me and Goodwin, the apartment of Pirates of the Caribbean is no longer an option for hosting an in-park sleepover. In 2017, the space was reimagined into an exclusive dining experience, 21 Royal. Technically, this experience is open to all guests, but it comes with a pretty hefty price tag: $18,000 for up to 12 guests. I guess that’s another item I’m definitely not going to cross off my bucket list!

From the sounds of the interview, Goodwin still has a few items on her own list that she hasn’t crossed off, like sleeping in the suite inside the castle. Considering the success of Zootopia 2, the reveal of the upcoming sequel Zootopia 3, and her love for all things Disney, I’m sure the Mouse will pull some strings and allow her access to the coveted spot one of these days. I just hope she takes lots of pictures and shares them with her nearly 450K followers.

If you’re local to Disneyland, you might be able to catch Ginnifer Goodwin enjoying the parks, but for those who aren’t, you can stream Once Upon a Time and both Zootopia films with an active Disney+ subscription.

#3661. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3660. Sony squeezes out a PlayStation 5 firmware update before the release of GTA 6

Sony has managed to squeeze out another PlayStation 5 firmware update before the highly-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto 6.

Sony has been rolling firmware updates out on a fairly regular basis, and like many of those updates, this latest one - version 26.07-14.23.00 - doesn't bring any very meaningful changes. Sony repeated the same "we've made some security fixes to the system software" patch-note that we've seen many times before.

And like all those firmware updates, 26.07-14.23.00 is mandatory for all PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles, assuming you want to go online or play the latest games. That, of course, includes GTA 6, which requires the console's firmware to be updated to its latest version before you can play.

The update should download automatically the next time you turn on your console, but you can also force the download through Settings > System > System Software > System Software Update and Settings. This is also where you can tick the option for your console to automatically download and install those updates in the future.

Although Sony hasn't directly said so, the high frequency of those security firmware updates is likely related to the impending release of GTA 6, especially in light of recent gen-AI-driven PS5 jailbreaks.

Any firmware released before GTA 6's release now becomes required to play the game, which delays potential security exploits, seeing as hackers would need to find vulnerabilities in that firmware in order to play. While this may never happen, Sony is at least trying to minimise the risk as much as possible.

GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

#3659. GTA 6 Won’t Get A 60 FPS Mode, Even On PS5 Pro, Because It’s ‘Not Powerful Enough’

30 FPSGrand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rockstar Games

Earlier this month, Rockstar Games confirmed Grand Theft Auto 6 targets 30 FPS on all platforms, even PlayStation 5 Pro. Before that news was revealed, I asked Rockstar if GTA 6 could receive a 60 FPS or even a 40 FPS mode in the future. And it sounds like, at least on current gen, that won’t be happening.

When Rockstar revealed that GTA 6 would target 30 FPS on PS5, PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X, and Xbox Series S, some players didn’t take it well. Many had hoped that Rockstar would, like so many other developers this console generation, offer some kind of performance mode. So for some, it was very sad news. But others held out hope that, perhaps in a post-launch update, Rockstar would add in a 60 FPS option or even a 40 FPS option for players enjoying the game on a 120hz TV.

However, Rockstar has confirmed with Kotaku that this isn’t going to happen, even on PS5 Pro. GTA 6 is just too much for these current consoles.

“Our base presentation makes use of ray-traced reflections and global illumination,” explained Technology Production Director Marc Chambers. “On the PS5 Pro, this is enhanced with the addition of ray-traced shadows, as well as overall added clarity through the use of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR). The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game’s visual fidelity. While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates.”

I’ve played over 130 hours of Grand Theft Auto 6 on PS5 Pro, and I don’t think the game is worse off for being locked to a framerate of 30 FPS. I’m somewhat of a framerate snob, but the gameplay in GTA 6 works totally fine at 30 fps. And the visuals are truly stunning, and more than make up for the lower framerate.

I know some people might suggest Rockstar turn off ray tracing and other fancy features to offer a 60 FPS option, but it would really take away from what the studio has built. GTA 6 is one of the best-looking games I’ve ever seen and easily sports the best-looking open world I’ve explored in my life. And a lot of that is down to the incredible lighting and ray-tracing tech that can be found in so many different parts of the world. Campfires cast orange, flickering glows on faces. Fancy red sports cars reflect the sunlight, tinting my crappy white car as I drive by them. The lights of my car’s dash and fuel gauge reflect in the windshield of my pickup truck as I cruise around the woods in the dark. Stuff like that adds a lot to the world and the vibes. Removing it would take away so much.

Even if you turn those visual features off, the game is still massive and incredibly alive, with dozens of planes in the air at all times, huge amounts of traffic, and multiple NPCs filling every frame of the game. So I’m not convinced it would be able to hit 60 FPS even with ray-tracing turned off or scaled back.

And hey, if history is any indicator of the future, this is the worst version of GTA 6 we’ll ever play. The game will almost certainly get ported to PC in the near future and run at 60 FPS or more over there, assuming your rig can run it. Later ports on next-gen machines in the future are also likely coming and will probably feature improved framerate options and more. So if you really want a 60 FPS option in GTA 6, you could just wait. But personally, I’m loving the game even at 30 FPS.

Unfortunately, this time you need to complete the main story—all 91 GTA 6 story missions —before you can access cheats and view their effects. After that, you'll have to complete the listed challenge to unlock each cheat command, though this does take into account what you've already done.

#3657. After GTA 6's original soundtrack, Justice probably won't work on any other video game ever again

You've probably heard at least a little bit of the Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack from French electronic duo, Justice: a single taken from the act's original soundtrack has been released as a standalone track, and was the accompaniment to GTA 6's launch trailer. Featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and the fantastic King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, it's clear that the duo - and Rockstar - have spared no expense on the production of music for the game.

From what we've heard so far, it's all very good: synth-drenched and poppy, a perfect mix of modern electronica and nostalgic throwback - ideal for the Miami-based setting of Vice City. You ought to enjoy the music while you can, though, because it seems Justice won't be coming back to video games any time soon. If ever.

Via a new interview with French publication Rockyrama, Justice's two members - Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay - shed a little light about their work with Rockstar, and their inspiration for joining the project. "When [the offer to work with Rockstar] arrived on the table, we thought 'if there’s one video game we have to do, it's this one.' As soon as we accepted and started working [on the OST], we thought it would probably be the first and last score we’ll ever do for a video game."

Interesting. The duo, from the clip we can see on Rockyrama's posts, don't seem to give more information about this decision - did they have a bad time working with Rockstar? Was it intense? Or is it rather down to the fact that, if you're going to work on a game, you may as well make it what is largely expected to be the biggest game of all time.

Justice, for what it's worth, consider the work they've done on GTA 6 to be "a real album" of music - it's not seen as lesser or different to the band, just because it's being released as part of a video game. "GTA 6 gave us the excuse and direction to do it. The music always had to be listenable on its own, even if each track is tailored for [a specific] scene," the band explains.

The band's album isn't the only music connected to the game, either. There's also a 34-song album launching for the game, composed of original songs from some of the biggest artists in the world. The album features Travis Scott, Rina Sawayama, Cardi B, Pinkpantheress, SZA, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Jennie, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson and many more. The full tracklist leaked at the weekend.

GTA 6 launches on Thursday, 19th November for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week

#3655. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3654. "Encouraging players to return is no mean feat" - Square Enix tempts Final Fantasy 14 players back with free game-time to fill void before new expansion

"People pause their adventures for all kinds of reasons."

Final Fantasy 14 is between expansions at the moment, with Evercold preparing for release in February. So, in order to keep the game populated for the next few months, Square Enix is running a special promotion in hopes of tempting players back in.

This promotion, which began yesterday, offers players a choice between two enticing freebies. Lapsed players who haven't logged in for over six months are to be given 30 days of free game time to hop back in and catch up with the main story quest ahead of Evercold's release.

In addition, there's an alluring character skip available too. If your FF14 character is at least level 90 on one class - the current level-cap is 100 - you can skip all the way to the final part of the latest Dawntrail expansion. You still need to grind to level 100 in preparation for Evercold, but the aforementioned free month of game time should provide plenty of time to do so.

In a producer letter written to accompany this promotion, Naoki Yoshida provided insight into why this was being implemented, stating that retaining players in an MMO like FF14 was of the "utmost importance".

"Encouraging players to return is no mean feat", Yoshida wrote. "People pause their adventures for all kinds of reasons, including dissatisfaction and loss of interest. Although we continually update the game to address such issues, the fact remains that getting players to resume their journey is a difficult task indeed.

"For one, I feel that the pace of change in our lives is growing increasingly fast. Back when A Realm Reborn launched, I set policies in place based on the idea that significant changes in life usually happened in roughly three-year cycles. With that in mind, we've done our best to avoid heavy-handed attempts to secure player retention through game design, and we still maintain that philosophy even today."

Yoshida went on to explain that promotions such as this are meant as a "tiny nudge". He notes that those who have retained subscriptions continuously remain "the most important" players in the development team's eyes, and acknowledges that the process of catching up in an MMO can seem "daunting" for many.

This problem of player retention is nothing new for MMOs, especially in the tricky time between the end of a current expansion and the beginning of a new one. MMO popularity often waxes and wanes, with a new expansion acting as an exciting call to action, with the months leading up to it often serving as a natural break-point for many. Still, monthly subs pay the bills, so keeping folks around even during these quiet months is important.

Final Fantasy 14: Evercold is looking like an especially exciting expansion. On top of the new story and two classes being added, the game is getting an overhaul to combat, with both classic Reborn and Evolved action modes, as well as a new raid difficulty meant to bridge the gap between normal and savage tiers.

The game has certainly come a long way since its initial release back in 2010. Dawntrail proved divisive among fans too, though with Evercold there's a lot of hope that a new overarching storyline can bring the steal back the hearts of players old and new.

#3653. It Took Me Over Three Hours To Walk Across GTA 6′s Massive Map

In some parts of the world, Grand Theft Auto 6 is out now on Xbox and PlayStation. And one of the biggest questions many players have is: How big is GTA 6‘s map? Well, I’ve walked, driven, and flown across the whole map to figure out just how long these journeys will take in Rockstar’s massive open-world sequel.

I doubt I need to explain what GTA 6 is or why so many people are excited to finally play it. So instead, let’s hop right into the numbers! First up, I walked across the whole map. To do this, I picked the most southern spot I could reach that was still on land and then made my way on foot as straight as possible without deviating. Sometimes, due to alligators or impossible-to-scale cliffs, I had to make small detours. And at first, I had to stick to highways as I worked my way up the islands that make up the bottom part of GTA 6‘s massive world. But once I got past that, I was able to mostly head north on foot without much issue. When I reached the furthest point north on the map, I stopped my timer.

It took me 3 hours, 21 minutes, and 20 seconds to walk across GTA 6. It was quite the journey, and during my walk I discovered areas I had never seen before and encountered new events, including a dude having sex with an anime character while wearing a VR headset.

After walking, I turned around and then ran across the map. I followed a similar route and also had to dodge alligators and other critters. Even running and sprinting constantly, it still took me 1 hour and 41 minutes. In comparison, running across GTA V‘s map takes about 30 minutes. And walking across it takes around two and a half hours. You might be wondering why I was able to run across GTA V‘s world in less than one-third the time I was able to run across GTA 6‘s, while walking didn’t result in quite so dramatic a discrepancy. I think it comes down to the fact that characters in GTA V can sprint forever and seem to move faster. In GTA 6, Jason and Lucia have a stamina bar that limits how far they can sprint at full speed and seem to move a bit slower.

Next up, I grabbed a mid-range sedan, hopped in as Lucia and, starting from the southernmost roadway on the map, I drove the highways and freeways all the way up to the most northern dirt road in the game. To drive across the map via the highway, it took 10 minutes and 53 seconds.

To be clear: I wasn’t following speed limits and I weaved around traffic like a lunatic. Still, it took nearly 11 minutes of highway driving at top speed to cross the whole map. In comparison, you can find videos of people driving quickly across GTA V‘s map in about eight minutes.

Finally, I grabbed a prop plane and flew from the furthest bit of land in the south to the furthest bit of land in the north of Leonida. This journey took 5 minutes and 51 seconds.

I imagine some people are going to use these numbers to try to compare this world to those of past GTA games. And some might be disappointed that GTA 6‘s map doesn’t take an hour to drive across. But trust me, as someone who has played over 130 hours of GTA 6, the map feels massive. I booted up GTA V recently to compare, and that game feels so tiny and empty in comparison.

These times also don’t do a good job of demonstrating how big GTA 6 is in every direction. There are more buildings to enter, underwater locations to explore, and large swaths of wilderness to explore. So while these numbers are interesting, they don’t tell the whole story.

If you were worried GTA 6 is small, just know that after playing 100 hours and finishing the story and most of the main side missions, I still have sections on my map I’ve yet to visit.
